articles.title: Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership and wider alliance against Trump threats
articles.description: Carney, top EU official push Canada associate membership and wider alliance against Trump threats AP News Carney points to EU's strong belief in democracy as political winds shift for 2 largest members CBC Canada’s Closer EU Ties Highlight the Impact of Trump’s Disdain Bloomberg.com Canada and Europe look beyond the US and China — but carefully POLITICO.eu At pivotal summit, Canadian-European security cooperation is
articles.content: MONTREAL (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the European Union’s top official pushed Thursday to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member” and build a broader alliance open to other countries as they warned of threats to sovereignty from economic coercion during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Speaking in Montreal on Thursday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would form the core of the proposed “Alliance for the Future,” but other like-minded countries would be welcome to join. Echoing Carney’s warning at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, von der Leyen said economic relationships once considered sources of stability were increasingly being used as instruments of pressure. “When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it is families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” she said. “We are seeing in real time our sovereignty being attacked.” Carney said the alliance would help Canada withstand economic shocks and prevent foreign governments and technology companies from dictating its choices. “Why does sovereignty matter in a dangerous and divided world? It allows us to withstand shocks,” Carney said at a news conference. “It allows us to live our lives as we choose.” Von der Leyen said the broader alliance would go beyond Canada’s potential associate membership, focusing on critical minerals, resilient supply chains, defense and security. “This is a wider concept,” she said at a business roundtable alongside Carney. “Other like-minded trusted partners are welcome.” Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. Asked Wednesday about possible retaliation, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the closer relationship was not directed against the United States but reflected longstanding shared interests. The White House said Thursday that U.S. trade and commerce officials had held discussions with their Canadian counterparts in recent days. The statement came in response to a question about Canada’s pursuit of closer ties with the EU. Carney played down the importance of the “associate member” designation, which von der Leyen continues to champion despite resistance from some European governments. “This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he said. Carney later used the term “associate member” himself while sitting beside von der Leyen at a business roundtable, emphasizing the economic opportunities closer cooperation could create. The summit puts Carney’s vision for a new global order to the test. At Davos, he warned that the U.S.-led international order was breaking down and economic integration was increasingly being weaponized. He urged middle powers to unite against coercion by more powerful countries. “We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old-world order,” von der Leyen said Thursday. “We need to imagine partnerships that are built on trust and driven by common interests and beliefs. As Mark Carney has said, the international order will also be built from Europe, with Canada as part of it.” Some EU member states have questioned the “associate member” designation proposed last month by von der Leyen, but she showed no sign Thursday of abandoning the idea. “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” she said. “This is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.” Von der Leyen described the proposed relationship as an “association without accession,” saying it could bring Canada closer to EU membership than any previous arrangement with a country outside the bloc. Anand Sundar, a special adviser at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France and Germany are among the countries unhappy with the designation and that it may not survive the summit. “The fact that member states have rejected the associate membership framing is very embarrassing for von der Leyen,” Sundar said. Carney has ruled out formally joining the EU and said any enhanced partnership would face a vote in Canada’s Parliament. The summit is expected to launch an “Alliance for the Future,” a framework for closer cooperation on trade, defense, critical minerals, technology and research. Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would finalize an agreement Friday giving Canadian companies, startups and researchers access to Europe’s network of 12 supercomputers, strengthening cooperation on artificial intelligence. Carney announced Thursday that Canada would invest up to C$1.6 billion ($1.1 billion) in Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere, which announced plans in April to merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha. He said Cohere would remain Canadian and invest at least C$1.7 billion ($1.2 billion) in new computing infrastructure in Canada. Carney said Canada would not wait for the future of artificial intelligence to be decided elsewhere by people it does not know or trust. Von der Leyen announced plans to strengthen strategic supply chains and encourage joint investment in industries critical to economic security. Canada is the only non-European country participating in the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($167-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, allowing Canadian companies to take part in joint European military purchases. But deeper defense cooperation faces obstacles. Sundar said France is pushing for strict “Made in Europe” rules that could limit Canadian companies’ access to future EU defense spending, while Germany favors broader participation. The two sides already have a sweeping free trade agreement, known as CETA, that eliminated most tariffs. The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025. Carney wants to double exports to other countries over the next decade. Canada and the EU are seeking closer cooperation on critical minerals as both sides work to diversify supply chains. Von der Leyen said the value of EU imports of Canadian critical raw materials rose 62% last year to 3.3 billion euros (C$5.18 billion), including lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite. Tobias Gehrke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said the disagreement over terminology was unlikely to derail closer cooperation. “There is no magic shortcut to rapidly reducing Europe’s and Canada’s reliance on the U.S. economy and military — not least since Washington might retaliate,” Gehrke said. “But the political window is now wide open to take a much bigger step than was previously conceivable.”

Bodies of 2 Colorado students and aspiring outdoorsmen are recovered after they died on hiking trip
articles.description: Bodies of 2 Colorado students and aspiring outdoorsmen are recovered after they died on hiking trip AP News 2 College Students Are Found Dead on a Colorado Mountain The New York Times 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Chaffee County Sheriff says missing Colorado Mountain College hikers have been found dead KKTV Two Colorado coll
articles.content: The bodies of two Colorado college students who died during a weekend hiking trip were recovered by helicopter Thursday after gusty winds delayed efforts to bring them down, police said. Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, were found Wednesday in a snow-filled basin of West Apostle Mountain. Ground crews helped recover their bodies around 1 p.m. the following day, the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office reported. Matsuda and Donlon set out last Friday from Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus for what was supposed to be a weekend trip to Ice Mountain, a 13,958-foot (4,254-meter) peak, and went missing. It was raining when they started hiking, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office, and despite a break in the weather Saturday morning, a severe storm arrived that afternoon, dumping up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of snow. Two college students have been found dead after going missing during a mountain hike. AP correspondent Mike Hempen reports. They were expected back by Sunday, but college staff reported them missing Monday morning, and their bodies were ultimately located in a basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Aspen. The bodies were taken to the coroner’s office, with autopsies scheduled for Monday. “They came here to learn, to explore and to build their futures,” Ben Cairns, the school’s campus dean, said in a statement. “Their lives were full of promise, and their loss is felt deeply by the students, faculty and staff who knew them.” Colorado Mountain College, which has campuses throughout the Colorado Rockies, is known for its programs focusing on the state’s robust outdoor recreation economy, including mountaineering, ski patrol and guiding careers. Matsuda, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Donlon, of Queensbury, New York, became fast friends at the small campus in Leadville, which bills itself as America’s highest city at 10,119 feet (3,084 meters) above sea level. Located about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Denver, the city is home to about 2,600 people and is flanked by some of Colorado’s tallest mountains. Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter. Classmates and faculty members described him as kind, intelligent and welcoming, the statement from the college said. Donlon, an avid climber and skier, was studying outdoor recreation leadership and had come to Colorado to pursue his love of the mountains. Ski or Die NY, a group of upstate New York skiers, called Donlon “one of the most ambitious skiers on the East Coast.” It said on its website that he became the youngest person to complete a strenuous 28-mile (45-kilometer) ski tour in the area’s High Peaks last December. “He lived life with a passion that was contagious, embodying everything we love about skiing in New York,” the group posted on social media. “He was a friend, an adventurer, and someone who was always hungry for what was next.” Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich credited Matsuda and Donlon with being capable, strong and prepared, saying in a social media post, “Almost all the safety measures we tell backcountry explorers to use, these men did.” “We are proud of these young men concerning how prepared they were, but sometimes mother nature throws you a curveball,” he said. Jason Marsteiner, the founder of The Survival University, a Colorado company that teaches wilderness skills, noted how quickly the weather can turn in the state’s high mountains. “The weather rolls in fast and the mountains are steep,” he said. “It’s an unforgiving environment.” About 60 search and rescue volunteers, aided by helicopters, drones and dogs, searched for the two men. The helicopter crew discovered a tent collapsed under the snow Tuesday with their sleeping bags, a stove and clothing near a lake northwest of Ice Mountain — but the students were nowhere to be found. Based on the tent’s location, Rohrich said it appeared Matsuda and Donlon changed plans and were aiming for the 13,597-foot (4,144-meter) West Apostle Mountain, instead of Ice Mountain. He said the location of the bodies, about a mile from their tent, indicated that they were well into a hike when they died. The sheriff’s office said their climbing equipment was not in their dorms, tent or vehicle, suggesting that they left their tent prepared for a technical climb. Trash inside the tent indicated that they ate before starting their hike, officials said. Authorities had been concerned that aerial searches could be limited in upcoming days because of poor weather that was expected to begin Friday. Johnson reported from Seattle, and Yu from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

articles.title: Michiganders, challengers, poll watchers head to early voting sites
articles.description: Early voting is well underway with only days left before the general election on Nov. 3. According to the Michigan Secretary of State, almost 1.4 million Michiganders had cast their […]
articles.content: Early voting is well underway with only days left before the general election on Nov. 3. According to the Michigan Secretary of State, almost 1.4 million Michiganders had cast their ballots as of Oct. 27. Early in-person voting opened up statewide on Oct. 24 and ends the Sunday before Election Day. Some locations, like the Foster Community Center in Lansing and the Hannah Community Center in East Lansing, offer early in-person voting until Nov. 2. Since opening on Oct. 24, poll workers at the Hannah Community Center have seen a steady stream of voters, either submitting their ballot or registering for the first time. “We’ve been a little bit under 200 or a little bit over 200,” said Susan Godfrey, an East Lansing precinct chair who has worked elections since 2011. Godfrey said more than a thousand people have voted at the location so far. Along with Michiganders looking to cast their ballots, Godfrey said groups of election challengers have been at the site all week. “I have had some of them stay the whole day,” she said, “some of them stay half a day, and then someone comes in and relieves them.” Challengers from Michigan’s Democratic and Republican parties, as well as the Promote The Vote Fund, were at the Hannah Community Center this week, Godfrey said. The presence of election challengers and poll watchers at a polling site is a standard part of any election, though they play different roles. Challengers are appointed by a credentialed organization, usually a political party. Poll watchers are members of the public and are limited to simply observing the election process. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) notified seven Michigan municipalities earlier this month, including Lansing and East Lansing, that election monitors will be stationed at certain polling locations on Election Day. State officials have reassured voters that monitors will act according to state law, but have encouraged early voting nonetheless. Godfrey said DOJ monitors will act as poll watchers. “East Lansing is really transparent with what we’re doing, and we are confident that we are following all the rules and regulations.” At the Foster Community Center, just over 1,500 people voted early and in-person, according to Gabriel Byrd Johnson, a Lansing precinct chair. In the community center’s parking lot, Robin Young and Emily Kress sat in lawn chairs. They are volunteers with the Ingham County Democratic Party, handing out voting guides. “We are just encouraging people, talking to them if they want to know about the candidates,” Young said. The voting guides listed all of the Democratic candidates on the ballot, but Young said the two were there to celebrate the process. “I think more than anything else, you need to make yourself an informed voter, because it’s a government for the people and by the people,” she said, “and by the people means getting involved.” The Hannah Community Center is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. until Nov. 1, and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Nov. 2 for early in-person voting. The Foster Community Center is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. until Nov. 1, and 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Nov. 2 for early in-person voting. Michiganders can check their early voting location on the Secretary of State’s website.

articles.title: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
articles.description: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing AP News After AI uproar, Dartmouth’s top academic official steps down The Boston Globe Dartmouth Provost’s Resignation May Set a Precedent for AI Transparency The Chronicle of Higher Education Senior official at Dartmouth College resigns over AI use The Washington Post Dartmouth provost resigns after review finds he used AI to
articles.content: A top administrator at Dartmouth College has resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, including in a guest column in The Washington Post on AI cheating. The announcement Wednesday of Provost Santiago Schnell’s departure from the Ivy League university comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools. Dartmouth touts itself as the birthplace of AI, saying the field got its start at the school in Hanover, New Hampshire, in 1956 when a small group of scientists gathered for a summer research project on the topic. A conference commemorating the 70th anniversary — titled “What Must Remain Human?” — began Thursday. University President Sian Leah Beilock said in a written statement that keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI means “leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing.” “That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars,” the president wrote, adding that Schnell’s departure was “his decision” and that the school wishes him well. Schnell referred questions to his attorneys, who didn’t immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment. Issues arose after the news outlet Semafor ran guest columns in major newspapers through an AI filter. Schnell’s August column in the Post, titled “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem,” was found to be entirely written by AI. Schnell defended himself, saying at the time he used ChatGPT to “refine a few arguments” but that the column was based on his “own thinking.” The college paper, The Dartmouth, then ran other publications from Schnell through an AI detector. Writing that predated ChatGPT’s 2022 public release was found to be human-written, but high rates of AI use were detected in his recent writing. Schnell told the paper in an email last month that he uses AI for “language refinement, copyediting, improving clarity and organization and making writing processes more efficient.” The paper ran the statement through an AI-detector and found it was AI-written. In a follow-up statement, Schnell told the paper that he “developed the substance and wrote a draft” of the email, then “used an AI tool to assist with language and clarity.” An investigation ensued, and the faculty committee found that Schnell used AI to “meaningfully alter his writing” and “was not forthcoming about his AI use.” Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously taught and held leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan and Indiana University, according to his LinkedIn profile. articles.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
articles.description: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
articles.content: Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said. Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says. As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies. Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said. AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards. Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company. articles.title: FACT FOCUS: Misinformation about voting spreads less than a week before Election Day
articles.content: False and misleading claims about the voting process are being spread online as voters cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms, with Election Day less than a week away. The posts often focus on alleged election rigging or voter fraud. However, closer scrutiny of the claim typically reveals a logical explanation. CLAIM: A punched hole in a Ventura County, California, ballot return envelope is proof of election rigging. THE FACTS: This is false. The ballot return envelopes have two holes, according to election officials. They help election workers confirm that the ballot has been removed and act as an accessibility feature. A video spreading online shows the front of a return envelope from Ventura County that has a punched hole on one side. A man explains that if ballots are inserted with a certain side facing the front of the envelope, the bubble for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is visible through the hole. The man warns: “Be very careful how you place your ballot in your California envelope.” A popular X post claimed that “California is rigging elections,” using the video as alleged proof. Simone Seydoux, spokesperson for the Office of the Ventura County Clerk-Recorder & Registrar of Voters, explained that the envelopes follow a design standard recommended by the California secretary of state. Both holes can be seen from the back of the envelope. They appear on each side of the spot voters must sign, acting as a guide for those who are vision impaired. One of these holes goes through the entire envelope so that election workers can ensure it is empty after the ballot has been removed. Workers also secure stacks of emptied envelopes for storage by inserting zip ties through this hole. “The holes are NOT positioned in order to see the vote on a particular contest,” Seydoux wrote in an email. “The envelopes are ordered ahead of time and used from one election to another if possible.” Ventura County’s 2026 general election ballot consists of three double-sided ballot cards, according to Seydoux. She added that “voters are welcome to fold the ballot and place it in the envelope in any order.” The California secretary of state’s office confirmed earlier this month that there is nothing untoward about such holes. “The small holes on some county ballot return envelopes are an accessibility feature to allow sight-impaired voters to orient themselves to where they are required to sign the envelope,” the office wrote in an Instagram post. “If a voter is concerned their ballot choices might be visible through these holes, they can insert their ballots into the return envelope in various ways where all choices are hidden.” CLAIM: A New York City polling site gave a voter two ballots, one of which was missing the conservative candidates. THE FACTS: This claim was originally made in a TikTok video by a user who says in the comments that she voted at the Borough of Manhattan Community College in New York City. A sample ballot for that location shows that it consists of two double-sided pages. One side of the second page includes judicial races, in which no conservative candidates are running. “They’re betting on your stupidity and they’re betting on your ignorance that you are not going to see that they’re giving you a ballot that is missing half the candidates,” the woman in the video says. “That’s actually some real foolery and real trickery right there. So honestly, wake up, wake up, wake up, wake up.” There are four judicial races on the ballot. Democratic candidates are running in all of them and Working Families Party candidates are running in one. There are no Republican or Conservative Party candidates listed since there are none in the race. “The only reason there would be no candidate on a party line in a contest on the ballot is because no individual was nominated by that party for that particular office,” Kathleen McGrath, a spokesperson for the New York State Board of Elections, wrote in an email. “Of course, all contests offer voters a space for write-in candidates, so voters can write in another person if they do not like the choices printed on the ballot.” She added that New York City has had multi-page ballots for many years. The woman in the video also highlights the fact that she was told she didn’t need to show her ID before voting. In New York, voters provide their Department of Motor Vehicles number or the last four digits of their social security number when registering to vote. They may also use another form of valid photo ID or a government document that shows their name and address, such as a utility bill or a bank statement. Voters will be asked for ID at the polls if their identity cannot be verified before Election Day, according to the state’s registration form. McGrath explained that voters must only verify their identity at the polls via signature if additional identification, such as a photo ID, has already been verified. Their signature is reviewed and approved by two bipartisan poll workers at the site to ensure it matches what is in their voter record. “Unfortunately, much mis- and disinformation about elections and voting spreads quickly online,” she wrote. “Worse yet, many social media posts are made solely as efforts to troll or get clicks (with no concern for truth or impact). Sometimes, it is simply the individual not understanding the process — which is run securely, transparently, and always by bipartisan officials in New York State. Boards of elections remain the trusted sources for accurate information.” CLAIM: Touchscreen voting machines in multiple states are flipping votes from Democrats to Republicans. THE FACTS: Election officials say the touchscreen challenges are almost always the result of user error or an easily fixed screen miscalibration, and say the number of complaints this year isn’t higher than it has been in years past, despite outsized attention on social media. They emphasize that voters can select a candidate as many times as needed, consult a poll worker for help and review selections before submitting their ballot. “Almost all of the claims of vote flipping are understandable human error,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, who noted disinformation purveyors often seize on well-meaning concerns to sow doubt in the voting process. “Is there one of us who hasn’t had a butt dial or mistyped something on our phones? It is not nefarious.” Voters across the country cast ballots in various ways, including with ballot marking devices that print a paper record or with paper ballots they fill out by hand. The counties where most of the recent vote-flipping social media reports are concentrated use ExpressVote ballot marking devices from a company called Election Systems & Software. The machines let voters make their selections on a touchscreen. Then, a paper record is typically printed for review before the votes are tabulated. Katina Granger, senior manager of public relations for the Nebraska-based ES&S, said the company works closely with election officials and provides technical support when needed but has not been made aware of any widespread issue with voting machines this cycle. She said when a voter is having difficulty, they should ask a poll worker for assistance. If they’ve already printed a ballot that doesn’t reflect their intended selections, “they should notify a poll worker rather than cast it so the jurisdiction can follow its procedures for replacing the ballot.” CLAIM: Ballots marked by poll workers will be disqualified in the 2026 midterm elections. THE FACTS: Voting procedures vary by jurisdiction, but it is not unheard of for poll workers to mark ballots as part of the process. There are multiple reasons a poll worker might write on a ballot, according to election officials in multiple states. Experts advise voters to check what the rules are in their district and to avoid making stray marks of their own. In many North Carolina counties, for example, election workers write “P” for provisional or “A” for absentee in a box in the upper left corner of a ballot so that they can be identified if they are put into a tabulator instead of sealed in an envelope as they are supposed to be. Ballots in Illinois are initialed before they are issued to voters. “I always like to say, get your facts straight from the source, and the source is your local election official,” said Pamela Smith, president and CEO of Verified Voting, a nonpartisan group focused on election technology. “Not your friends, cousin, uncle, on Facebook.” Smith encouraged voters to seek out information on the websites or social media accounts of those officials. She also suggested asking a poll worker who marks a ballot why they’ve done so if a voter has concerns. Find AP Fact Checks here: https://apnews.com/APFactCheck.

articles.title: Detroit’s election chief expects November 2026 turnout to surpass 2022
articles.description: Winfrey said she feels confident this election will run "as smoothly and safely as previous elections."
articles.content: Detroit election officials project a 40-45% to turnout for the November general election, City Clerk Janice Winfrey said at a Thursday announcement at the Department of Elections. Detroit has about registered 532,000 voters, Winfrey said. The projection compares with a 34% turnout in the 2022 midterm election, said Daniel Baxter, chief of operations for the city’s elections department. “Those trends are reflective of the 2018 election. If you remember that election, that was a non-incumbent election, and the city of Detroit had a 42% turnout. So we’re seeing that same synergy in Detroit,” Baxter said, adding that he looks at empirical data to estimate turnout. “We looked at 2014, 2022, and 2018, and then we looked at our absentee votes. That’s the best indicator of what we anticipate regarding turnout. So when we looked at absentee voting, we looked back at the 2022 election and saw that we had … 80,000 absentee ballots that were returned for that particular election. And then we also looked at our early votes, and then the synergy associated with this upcoming election,” Baxter said. As of Oct. 28, 10,000 voted early. Winfrey expects 25,000-30,000 early voters. Winfrey said the city issued 106,000 absentee ballots and 60,000 have been returned, though she anticipates counting up to 80,000 ballots by Election Day. She urges voters to drop off their ballots at one of 38 drop boxes across the city, early voting centers or the city’s Department of Elections. “We’ve seen an uptick of in the use of our drop boxes. That’s good by design. We’ve increased the number of drop boxes because we know you can depend on those drop boxes. You can depend on us being able to receive those ballots,” Winfrey said. Pre-tabulation began Oct. 26 in Hall A at Huntington Place, and about 27,000 ballots have been tabulated thus far, Winfrey said. She expects 105,000 to 125,000 voters to cast their ballots at precincts. The U.S. Department of Justice’s (DOJ) is planning to send federal monitors at polling places in Detroit. Winfrey said the DOJ will provide the city the number of monitors it plans to send out by Friday. She and other officials said they do not expect to run into security issues at polls. “We’re ready, and we want you to know that we administer secure, accessible and accurate elections, and we need you to participate,” Winfrey said. Federal monitors have been present in Michigan for several past federal elections, according to the state. However, like any other poll watcher, DOJ monitors cannot speak with voters, touch election equipment or ballots, or interfere with the administration of the election. Winfrey said she feels confident this election will run “as smoothly and safely as previous elections. Baxter added that the clerk and elections department officials are in constant communication with the city’s Corporation Counsel Conrad Mallett, who appeared at Winfrey’s announcement and touted her efforts to organize the election. “We have not had any disruptions and there has been no indication that we are expecting to see anyone try to disrupt the process,” Mallett said. On Nov. 4, free bus rides and paratransit services will be available through the Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) to take riders to the polls. No identification will be required and anyone can hop on the bus on Election Day for free rides, even if they have already voted. Paratransit riders can book their rides in advance, said Robert Cramer, director of DDOT. “To learn more about how to find the schedule and check the real-time arrival status, I really encourage everyone who hasn’t already to download the transit app. It’s a free app,” Cramer said. Dana Afana is the Detroit city hall reporter for the Free Press. Contact: dafana@freepress.com. Follow her: @DanaAfana. Your email address will not be published. articles.title: Clinton Twp. man held on a $1 million bond for allegedly ramming Fraser police vehicle
articles.content: A Clinton Township man is being held on a $1 million cash bond after he was accused of ramming a Fraser police car during a chase earlier this week that ended when the driver lost control of his car and crashed into a pond. Gaspare Cracchiolo, 61, was arraigned Wednesday, Oct. 28 in 39th District Court in Roseville on two felony counts of assault with intent to do great bodily harm less than murder, and other crimes. Judge Joseph Boedeker set bond at $1 million cash or surety. “Public safety is our top priority,” said Macomb County Prosecutor Pete Lucido. “We must protect those who put their lives on the line to protect us and ensure that anyone who threatens the safety of our community is held accountable.” According to police and prosecutors, Fraser police on Monday, Oct. 26 received information about a vehicle that allegedly was involved in a hit-and-run and felony fleeing and eluding incident. Officers located the vehicle behind a business on Kelly Road near Groesbeck Highway in Fraser and attempted to conduct a traffic stop. Prosecutors said the suspect vehicle intentionally drove into the driver’s side door of the patrol cars with the officers inside. The two officers suffered minor injuries, including arm and knee pain for one officer, and back and leg pain for the other. The officers were able to exit their patrol vehicle through the passenger side door and ordered the driver to stop. The driver put his car in reverse and drove out of the parking lot and fled the scene, according to investigators. Other Fraser officers located the vehicle and pursued it for several miles. The pursuit came to an end when the driver lost control and overturned the vehicle into a retention pond near Groesbeck and 11 Mile Road in Warren. The driver was taken into custody after being medically cleared. He is also charged as a habitual offender, which comes into play during sentencing. Cracchiolo is scheduled to return to court for a probable cause conference on Nov. 13. Ironically, Cracchiolo took to social media in March to blast a Warren district court judge who is charged with operating while intoxicated and crashing into a SMART bus. On his Facebook page, he referred to the judge as a “piece of s—” jurist “who thinks he above the law and thinks he can get away with drunk driving with his actions …. because he’s a judge !!” The post was an apparent reference to 37th District Judge John Chmura, who faces charges from an incident in March when he was involved in a crash in Sterling Heights. Chmura is scheduled to stand trial on Nov. 16.

South Korean prosecutor seeks death penalty for ex-President Yoon over martial law debacle
articles.content: SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — A South Korean special prosecutor on Thursday demanded the death penalty for ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol, ahead of an appeals court verdict on rebellion charges over his brief imposition of martial law in December 2024. The Seoul High Court has yet to set a date for a verdict on Yoon’s appeal of a life sentence handed down in February by the Seoul Central District Court. The court found that he illegally mobilized troops and police to seize the legislature, arrest political opponents and establish unchecked rule for a “considerable time.” Investigators led by Special Prosecutor Cho Eun-suk also appealed the ruling, arguing Yoon deserves the death penalty because his actions posed a grave threat to the country’s democracy. An execution would be unlikely. South Korea has not executed anyone since 1997, effectively maintaining a moratorium on capital punishment following calls for its abolition. During the hearing at the high court, Cho’s team said only the death penalty could fully hold Yoon accountable for a crime as serious as orchestrating a rebellion and that the country’s long-standing pause on executions should not prevent courts from imposing death sentences. Yoon’s legal team told reporters that prosecutors were repeating an argument “devoid of evidence and legal logic” and claimed that Yoon’s martial law was intended to raise public awareness about what he called attempts by the opposition-led legislature to paralyze state affairs. It said Yoon had no intention of causing harm or establishing authoritarian rule. Yoon’s martial law decree, announced late at night on Dec. 3, 2024, lasted only hours until a quorum of lawmakers broke through a blockade of heavily armed soldiers and police at the National Assembly and voted to overturn it, forcing his Cabinet to lift the measure. Yoon was suspended from office on Dec. 14, 2024, after being impeached by the liberal-led legislature and was formally removed by the Constitutional Court in April 2025. He was re-arrested in July 2025 and has faced multiple criminal trials over the martial law debacle and other allegations, with the rebellion charge carrying the heaviest punishment. In addition to appealing his life sentence for rebellion, Yoon has also appealed a 30-year prison term in a case accusing him of ordering drone flights in 2024 to deliberately heighten tensions with North Korea and create a pretext for martial law at home. Yoon’s lawyers said the drone flights were a response to North Korea flying thousands of trash-carrying balloons into the South.
